list.listitem: Seek immediate transport to a medical facility for any suspected snake or scorpion envenomation; keep the patient calm and comfortable.
Monitor vital signs and symptoms of progressive deterioration enroute to the medical facility to aid in determining the severity of the envenomation. C
Obtain and reconstitute antivenom as appropriate (CroFab has less risk for reactions than Antivenin (Crotalidae) Polyvalent [ACP]). C
Consult an intensive care unit and snake envenomation expert. Call the Poison Control Center (1-800-222-1222) for advice and resource information if snake envenomation expert is not available. C

background.definition: Bites from venomous snakes are relatively uncommon but can be fatal especially under unfavorable conditions of poor health and great distance from medical care. The most dangerous North American snakes are Crotalinae (rattlesnakes, copperheads, and cottonmouths) and Elapidae (coral snakes). Most scorpion stings result in localized pain and inflammation. The Buthidae family of scorpions are the most venomous and most dangerous, accounting for an estimated 5000 deaths annually worldwide. In the United States, the bark scorpion, Centruroides exilicuada, is potentially fatal.

list.listitem: The exact incidence of venomous snake bites is unknown; as a significant number are not reported.

Reports from the CDC in 2018, estimate around 7000 bites per year with five fatalities in the USA. Although most bites are not fatal, 10%-44% of victims suffer some form of permanant injury or disabilty
The incidence of snakebites varies in national centers across the United States from 4 bites to 19 bites per 100,000 of the population.
Mishandling of a captive venomous snake
Tormenting or trying to capture a cornered venomous snake
Exposure to natural habitats
Sleeping outdoors in a natural habitat and not checking clothes and shoes prior to putting them on
Most bites result from accidental exposure, especially among outside workers such as farmers, landscapers, gardners, and mechanics
Snake venoms are highly complex enzymes, glycoproteins, low-molecular-weight polypeptides, minerals, and perhaps other yet unidentified substances.

Anticoagulation effects, as well as procoagulant effects of consumptive coagulopathy, cause significant swelling and ecchymosis. In severe cases, pulmonary hemorrhage, as well as variable multisystem organ failure due to leakage or hemorrhage, occurs.
Scorpion venom contains mucopolysaccharides, hyaluronidase, protease inhibitors, histamine releasers, and neurotoxins that can cause excessive neuromuscular activity and autonomic dysfunction.
Envenomation occurs with most Crotalinae (rattlesnake, copperhead, cottonmouth) and all Elapidae (coral snake) bites. C

In snake envenomation, advancing symptoms from a localized reaction to systemic whole body signs requires emergency transportation while documenting the rate of change by measuring the limb circumference every 15 minutes. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Multiple rows of tiny puncture wounds
Intense burning pain at puncture site
Two fang marks but a glancing blow may only leave one mark

list.listitem: Typically, the patient is aware of a snake bite. What may be unknown is the type of snake, or whether it was a "dry" bite (lacking venom), which can happen 1 out of 5 times. Coral snake bites usually result in envenomation even without fang marks.

It is important to attempt to identify the snake either by visualization (by someone with experience in identifying snakes) or by taking a digital photograph. A 3-step identification method may be helpful in differentiating venomous from nonvenomous snakes in North America. Killing the snake is not recommended as it wastes time and risks further injury to additional victims.

The patient is usually aware of snake bite/attack and has evidence of a puncture wound with severe local pain. Advancing edema, ecchymosis, and bleeding from the bite site follow. Envenomation can be confirmed by severe pain at the bite site within minutes, local and limb edema in the ensuing hours, and ecchymoses both localized and in more remote sites because of anticoagulant substances in the venom.

Systemic symptoms of nausea, emesis, weakness, an odd sense of taste, and perioral numbness may occur simultaneously. Signs of severe evenomation include tachycardia, tachypnea, respiratory distress, hypotension, and shock.
Vomiting, neurotoxicity, and elevated serum creatinine levels are significant predictors of mortality among inpatients with snake envenomation.

A systematic review found that the likelihood of severe systemic envenomation increased with time from bite to care of more than 6 hours; patient younger than age 12 years; large snake size; and ptosis.

Pain and paresthesias with mild scorpion envenomation are typical. Severe scorpion envenomation can result in multiple neurotoxic and cardiotoxic manifestations, including paresthesias, tremors, irritability, apprehension, ataxia, dysarthria, salivation, confusion, convulsions, delirium, pulmonary edema, and cardiac arrythmias; coagulopathies are rare.

Obtain baseline laboratory tests including CBC, complete metabolic profile, creatinine phosphokinase, and liver function tests, PT/INR/aPTT, fibrinogen, fibrinogen degradation products, D-dimer, and urinalysis for any suspected venomous snake bite.
Monitor PT and aPTT with venom-induced consumptive coagulopathy.
If severe envenomation, consider ECG, chest x-ray, and ABG to assess cardiac and pulmonary status.
X-rays of bites may reveal retained teeth or fangs.
Obtain CT of head for any altered level of consciousness, especially with severe coagulopathy.

The most reliable test is to measure the intracompartmental pressure directly though a cannula introduced into the compartment, however this should not be contemplated until patient is hemodynamically stable.

Unless you are absolutely sure that a snake bite is from a nonvenomous snake, transport the patient immediately to a medical center for emergency supportive care and antivenom treatment. Attempt to identify the snake by photograph or by visualization by an experienced individual. Do not attempt to kill or trap the snake.

Envenomation can be confirmed by severe pain at the bite site within minutes, local and limb edema in the ensuing hours, and ecchymoses both localized and in more remote sites due to anticoagulant substances in the venom.
Systemic symptoms of nausea, vomiting, numbness, respiratory distress, or hypotension suggest a serious envenomation.
Unless you are absolutely sure that a snake bite is from a nonvenomous snake, transport the patient immediately to a medical center for emergency supportive care and antivenom treatment. C
Provide intensive medical care for impending shock with 2 large bore IV sites for crystalloid infusions, and supportive management of airway, breathing, and circulation. C
Immediately administrate antivenom according to the severity of symptoms and the manufacturer's recommendations for severe snake envenomation. C

For general approach to snake bite, see . Establish 2 large bore IV access sites for infusion of crystalloid fluids in case of shock. Consult a snake evenomation expert, if available, for treatment options.
Crotalidae (rattlesnake, copperhead, cottonmouth) antivenom is available in 2 forms: CroFab and ACP.

CroFab: Savage Labs, Melville, New York; ovine source, 4 North American pit viper venoms; 14.3% incidence acute allergic reaction; 3% incidence serum sickness; $2000 per 2 vials. Mild and moderate envenomation: 4 to 6 vials; severe envenomation: 6 vials; follow manufacturer's recommendations. CroFab Hotline: 1-87-SERPDRUG or 1-877-377-3784. Adverse events following CroFab administration are rare and generally not severe.

ACP: Wyeth-Ayerst Labs, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania; equine source, 4 North American pit viper venoms; 23% to 56% incidence acute allergic reaction; 18% to 86% incidence serum sickness; $900 per vial. Mild envenomation: up to to 5 vials; moderate envenomation: 10 vials; severe envenomation: 15 to 20 vials.

For Elapidae (coral snake) envenomations, an equine-based antivenom is available. Use slow IV administration with the physician at bedside to monitor for an allergic reaction. It may be useful to give routine prophylactic epinephrine for polyvalent antivenom to offset adverse reactions to ovine or equine sera.
A Cochrane review found no RCTs evaluating the efficacy and safety of snake antivenom for snake venom induced consumption coagulopathy.
Prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated for venomous snake bites.
No consensus protocol recommendation for severe scorpion envenomation is available. Some scorpion envenomation experts recommend high-dose IV scorpion polyvalent antivenom, if available.
An open-label randomized trial of 70 patients found that scorpion antivenom plus prazosin was more effective than prazosin alone in resolution of symptoms.
Premedication with adrenaline (epinephrine) containing preparations appears to be effective at reducing the incidence of early adverse reactions to snake antivenom.
Monitor advancing edema and symptoms by measuring and recording the circumference of the affected limb every 15 minutes.

Judicious fasciotomy may be appropriate if there is significant compartment syndrome due to excessive swelling and bleeding. Surgical wound care may create additional complications and is best used as a last resort to save a limb.

The victim is best handled by keeping them calm (slowing the heart rate will slow the circulation of venom); identifying the fang marks, which are typically 2 puncture wounds but may be just 1 in a glancing blow; local wound care; marking the advancing level of edema every 15 minutes; removing jewelry or tight-fitting clothes or apparatus; and most important, emergent transport to a local medical facility.
Tourniquets, suction, incision, ice, alcohol, folk remedies, and electric shock have no proven benefit and should be avoided.
Lymphatic compression bands and pressure immobilization techniques may inhibit the spread of venom but evidence of improved outcome is not clear.
Try to minimize activity of the victim. Some situations, such as remote back country hiking or camping trips, may require that the victim hike out if no one can carry him or her.

The factors that most decrease morbidity and mortality include immediate transportation and intensive medical care and antivenom for venomous snakebites. Supportive care and observation should be used for most scorpion stings in the Unites States with possible IV antivenom in severe envenomation (Centruroides genus in the southwest United States), though the literature is not entirely clear on an established protocol.
Death is rare but can occur with large, deep envenomations, delayed treatment, and comorbid conditions. C
Significant disability because of the deformity of a limb may occur. C
US antivenoms are US Food and Drug Administration category C (ie, of uncertain safety; animal studies show an adverse effect; no human studies).
Pregnant patients with a snake or scorpion bite should have an early evaluation by an obstetrician for fetal and placenta assessment.
Fetal malformation from snake venom has been described.
Anticoagulant and proteolytic effects of snake venom can disrupt the placental attachment to the uterus, causing placental abruption and miscarriage.
Early gestation, delayed treatment, and severe envenomation are risks for an unfavorable outcome.
Children may receive a higher dose per kilogram of body weight, which may present greater toxicity.
Children have a high risk of getting bit on the upper body because of their short stature, which causes quicker systemic effects of envenomation.

feature.caption: Overview of the Management of Snake Bite.*
feature.feature_body:
Snake Bite Signs and Symptoms Laboratory Findings Management
Nonenvenomation (ie, "dry bite") Fang marks, no clinical signs or symptoms No abnormalities Wound care Tetanus prophylaxis observe ≥8 hours
Mild envenomation Localized pain, swelling, ecchymosis, no systemic signs No abnormalities Wound care Tetanus prophylaxis observe ≥8 hours
Moderate envenomation Signs and symptoms extend beyond bite area. Systemic signs include paresthesias, perioral numbness, strange metallic taste, muscle weakness, and mild hypotension
Wound care Tetanus prophylaxis observe ≥8 hours ICU monitoring IV access CroFab 4-6 vials or ACP (10 vials)
Severe envenomation Rapidly involves entire body. Respiratory distress, shock, multiorgan failure, DIC, hemorrhage, death As above, plus: laboratory results consistent with: DIC, renal failure, or rhabdomyolysis Wound care Tetanus prophylaxis observe ≥8 hours ICU monitoring IV access Crofab 6+ vials or ACP 15-20 vials
*Urgent transport recommended for all patients unless nonvenomous snake can be positively identified. ACP denotes Antivenin (Crotalidae) Polyvalent; DIC: disseminated intravascular coagulopathy. 1Data from Angel MF, Zhang F, Jones M, Henderson J, Chapman SW. Necrotizing fasciitis of the upper extremity resulting from a water moccasin bite. South Med J 2002;95:1090-1094.
